 Deputy Governor's Welcoming Remarks at the DNFBP Compliance Conference 2026
 Welcoming Remarks by Deputy Governor Dato’ Marzunisham Omar
at the DNFBP Compliance Conference 2026
Sasana Kijang | 22 October 2026 
Distinguished guests, representatives of regulatory and supervisory agencies, professional bodies, industry associations, and members of Malaysia's Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions (DNFBP).
 It is my pleasure to welcome you to the DNFBP Compliance Conference 2026.
 This year marks an important milestone in Malaysia's fight against financial crime. Since the enactment of the Anti-Money Laundering Act in 2001. 25 years ago, we have spent a quarter century strengthening our laws, institutions and capabilities against money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.
 Over the 25 years, one lesson becomes increasingly clear. Regulators, law enforcement agencies and financial institutions cannot fight financial crime alone.
 Long before illicit funds reach financial system, a company may be incorporated. A transaction may be structured. A legal arrangement may be created. A professional service may be sought. Each of these moments, someone is standing at the gate .
 Malaysia therefore needs the judgement, diligence and professionalism of all those who help shape our corporate and legal landscape. This is why your presence today matters.
 Ladies and gentlemen,
Companies, trusts and legal arrangements, are essential to the economy. But they can be misused to disguise beneficial ownership, conceal origins of illegal proceeds or create a veneer of legitimacy around criminal activity. This places professional service providers, all of you in this room, in a critical position within our fight against financial crime.
 The recent conclusion of Malaysia's Mutual Evaluation reaffirmed the importance of this role. DNFBPs are not merely participants in the AML/CFT/CPF framework. You are well placed to detect, prevent and report illicit activities before they enter the financial system.
 This responsibility has never been more important. Financial crime is increasingly driven by highly organised criminal networks operating across borders. They leverage on technology, exploit legal structures and continuously adapt their methods. They study our controls and framework. They identify weaknesses and adjust approaches in response to our safeguards. When one avenue is closed, they quickly search for another. They continuously look for the gate where scrutiny is weakest .
 Across the region, we are seeing sophisticated criminal networks are increasingly exploiting professional services and legitimate business structures to conceal ownership, integrate illicit proceeds and make criminal activities appear legitimate. A recent Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia by UNODC identifies lawyers and accountants among the specialist facilitators within these criminal networks, operating on a contractual basis and providing enabling services to criminal organisations.
 Another emerging risk that deserves particular attention is the growing use of corporate mules. Data from the National Fraud Portal points to a rise in corporate mule accounts, reflecting how criminal networks are increasingly exploiting corporate entities to conceal illicit financial flows.
 Ladies and gentlemen,
Every ringgit that criminals successfully laundered strengthens criminal enterprises and weakens trust in our institutions. When a professional identifies suspicious activity, refuses to facilitate a questionable arrangement, or submits a suspicious transaction report, that professional is doing far more than meeting a regulatory requirement. They are closing a gate that criminals were attempting to enter . In doing so, you are helping to protect businesses, communities and our country.
 More than ever, professionals form a vital first line of defence against financial crime. This responsibility goes beyond procedural compliance, it requires professional scepticism, asking critical questions and challenging inconsistencies. And at times, the courage to say "no".
 Ultimately, effective gatekeeping depends on sound judgement. It is about understanding who your clients are, where their funds come from, and why certain transactions are being undertaken. The strength of our defences ultimately rests on the quality of those judgements.
 As professional services become increasingly digital, these responsibilities become even more critical. Digital onboarding, virtual business relationships and cross-border service delivery have improved efficiency and accessibility. But they also create new opportunities for criminals to conceal identities, misrepresent information and establish seemingly legitimate business relationships. In this environment, our vigilance must evolve alongside technology.
 Effective vigilance, however, goes beyond reviewing transactional activity. It requires a deeper understanding of customers, their business activities and the broader context in which they operate. This calls for a risk-based approach. One where professionals recognise behavioural, structural and situational red flags that may indicate potential misuse of their services.
 Ladies and gentlemen,
An effective AML/CFT/CPF framework depends not only on strong laws and sound policies, but also on credible supervision and enforcement. This is why Bank Negara Malaysia takes non-compliance seriously. Weaknesses in one part of the system can compromise the integrity of Malaysia's entire AML/CFT framework.
 Recent joint enforcement actions involving regulatory and law enforcement agencies reinforce this point. Bank Negara Malaysia and the Companies Commission of Malaysia recently took enforcement action against a company secretary for failing to submit suspicious transaction reports relating to foreign nationals suspected to be involved in an international scam syndicate.
 A Labuan investment bank was subjected to enforcement action by Bank Negara Malaysia and the Labuan Financial Services Authority following material deficiencies in customer due diligence that affect the firm’s ability to assess customer’s potential involvement in illicit overseas activities and delays in the submission of suspicious transaction reports.
 These cases may involve different sectors and circumstances, but they convey the same message: Weak due diligence, vigilance and reporting create space for criminals to operate. Professional services must never become the gate through which illicit funds acquire the appearance of legitimacy, whether knowingly or unknowingly.
 Compliance must therefore be viewed not simply as a regulatory obligation. It is a professional responsibility. Indeed, I would go one step further. AML/CFT compliance is part of the broader duty to uphold the trust placed in every profession represented here.
 With that trust comes responsibility. Every client you accept, every company you incorporate, every transaction you review, and every suspicious activity you report is an opportunity to protect the integrity of the system. Individually, these may appear to be routine decisions. But collectively they shape the integrity of Malaysia’s financial and corporate system.
 Ladies and gentlemen,
The fight against financial crime ultimately depends on cooperation. No regulator, law enforcement agency or professional service provider can succeed alone. Our defences are strongest when our different perspectives are connected. Only through strong partnerships, meaningful information sharing and collective vigilance can we effectively respond to increasingly sophisticated financial crime threats.
 This collaboration will become even more important as we move forward. In 2027, Bank Negara Malaysia will undertake the next iteration National Risk Assessment, which will enable a deeper assessment of the money laundering and terrorism financing risks facing the DNFBP sectors. The findings will support the development of more targeted policies, guidance, and mitigation measures tailored to the specific risks faced by each sector. Your practical insights will be essential. They will help ensure that our policy responses remain effective, proportionate and grounded in the realities faced by each sector.
 I would also like to express our sincere appreciation to relevant regulatory agencies, professional bodies and industry associations for their continued cooperation and support. In particular, we thank the Companies Commission of Malaysia, the Malaysian Bar Council, the Malaysian Institute of Accountants, as well as the various industry associations represented here today.
 Your work in promoting awareness, facilitating outreach and supporting capacity building has strengthened the resilience of the sector and the community. Let us now build on that partnership, not only by sharing information after risks materialise, but by identifying vulnerabilities earlier and managing them together.
 Let me conclude.
 Criminals will continue to evolve. They will become faster, more organised and more sophisticated. I have no doubt they will test our controls, exploit complexity and search for the weak points.
 But there is one thing they cannot easily overcome: A community of professionals committed to integrity. They cannot overcome professionals who ask critical questions. They cannot overcome a culture where suspicious activities are questioned rather than ignored. And they cannot overcome institutions that share information and act with a common purpose. In short, they cannot overcome a system in which every gate is guarded with sound good judgement, vigilance and courage .
 Let us leave this conference with a renewed sense of purpose, a stronger commitment to vigilance, and a shared determination to protect the integrity of Malaysia's financial and corporate system.
 Each of us stands at a different gate . But all of

 Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot
 Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot
 Given at the 2nd Annual Conference on Sustainable Finance at the Banco de México on 21 October 2026 
 Published on 
 23 October 2026
 James Talbot, Executive Director for International at the Bank of England and the Bank’s Executive Sponsor for climate, explains how physical climate shocks can affect inflation and output, and how central banks can assess and respond to them. He considers two connected horizons: their near-term effects on monetary policy, and the longer-term role of economic resilience, adaptation and insurance in helping economies absorb future shocks and support price and financial stability.
 Speech
 Physical shocks increasingly matter for central banks
 Governor, distinguished guests, I am sorry that I cannot be there with you in person at such a prestigious event. It is very much an honour and a pleasure, and my thanks to Dr. Fabrizio López-Gallo Dey for inviting me to speak today. 
 The physical impacts of climate change are becoming larger and more proximate, and their short-term economic impacts are also increasing. Annual global damages from weather-related events have more than doubled since the early 2000s, reaching over $200bn in 2025 footnote [1] .
 In light of that, the economic effects of climate change are increasingly on the radar of central bankers. When extreme weather events affect production, output and inflation, that matters for our primary goal of maintaining price stability. 
 Let me take two examples that are close to home:
 Increasingly high summer temperatures reduce water levels on key transport arteries for industrial trade, like the River Rhine in Germany. When water levels fall, ships reduce the amount of cargo they carry, disrupting the movement of goods and increasing transport costs. 
 Such exceptionally low water levels have become a recurring feature in recent years. The economic effects have also been material: recent research estimates that 30 days of low water on the Rhine reduces German industrial production by around 1% footnote [2] . 
 In October 2024, extreme rainfall caused devastating flash floods in Valencia. Aside from the tragic loss of human life, economic losses amounted to over 20% of regional GDP. Spanish Q4 GDP growth was reduced by between 0.1 and 0.2 percentage points footnote [3] .
 The economic impact would have been larger were it not for the high level of insurance protection for affected households and businesses. Around 250,000 insurance claims were filed following the floods and Spain's Insurance Compensation Consortium had paid more than €4bn in compensation by late 2025, making this the largest event the scheme has ever managed footnote [4] . 
 Even countries like the UK, which may be less susceptible to large physical shocks, can be affected by the impact of events abroad. 
 Over the past four years, as chair of the NGFS Workstream on Monetary Policy, I have worked together with more than sixty central banks to set out a framework to assess the impact of climate change on the economy, to measure its effects and to determine what monetary policymakers should do about it.
 I’ll talk today about how the physical impacts of climate change can affect the economy in the near term; how we diagnose their magnitude, persistence and propagation; whether their effects belong in the central forecast or in the risks around it; and how that diagnosis informs monetary policy judgements. We set out each of these steps in an NGFS guide for monetary policymakers that we published earlier this year footnote [5] .
 I also want to look beyond the near-term policy horizon. In particular, how repeated losses, adaptation, fiscal space and insurance protection gaps shape the capacity of economies and financial systems to absorb future shocks.
 I will argue that these two horizons are connected: The resilience an economy has built determines the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic impact of a shock over the monetary-policy horizon. And, in turn, repeated shocks can erode that resilience over the longer term, eventually exacerbating the effects of climate shocks when they occur.
 How physical shocks transmit through the economy
 Let me start with how physical shocks can affect the economy. 
 Physical hazards can operate through several channels at once: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains. They can weaken demand and confidence among economic agents, tighten credit conditions and raise uncertainty. 
 Importantly for monetary policymakers, those channels can interact and may also move output and inflation in different directions, making the policy response more challenging.
 But different physical hazards can transmit through the economy in different ways. To give some examples footnote [6] :
 Heatwaves transmit as a shock to productive capacity and labour supply. They push down on GDP while increasing inflation volatility, making them relevant for monetary policy even though direct physical damage is not as visible as for a flood or storm. 
 Droughts reduce productive capacity in agriculture pushing down on production and up on prices. They can raise inflation both through the effect on domestic production and through more expensive imports. 
 Floods and cyclones damage the capital stock, reducing demand and investment, which can in turn push down on output and inflation. But floods can also be inflationary where they hit food supply, logistics or essential infrastructure.
 So while there is no one-size-fits-all pattern for the effects of a physical shock, there are some common themes:
 Shocks are often transmitted through a disruption to production;
 That usually means that output and inflation often move in opposite directions; and
 Even when shocks occur overseas, these can be transmitted through changes to exports and commodity prices, particularly for open economies. Indeed, a 2022 study for the euro area showed that for every 1% unanticipated increase in globally traded food prices, overall inflation rose by 0.1% footnote [7] . 
 This latter channel is also particularly important for the UK since we import around 40% of our food. In recent work at the Bank of England, we have looked at the impacts of extreme weather events on commodity prices and UK inflation footnote [8] . The estimates from the model suggest that global weather-related disruption has played a non-trivial role in UK food and headline inflation over the past two decades 
 This makes climate-related shocks relevant to our regular inflation forecasting. Indeed, many central banks are now assessing the impact of food, energy, supply-chain, and weather-related shocks. That is because these shocks are affecting inflation and output forecasts, or the risks around them, in an increasingly meaningful way . 
 The NGFS note on the economic and financial impacts of extreme weather events, produced for the 2026 French G7 Presidency, uses 31 case studies to show that these effects repeatedly appear in output, employment and prices across a geographically diverse range of countries footnote [9] . Supply-chain and trade linkages can also propagate these shocks beyond the country or region directly affected. 
 With that in mind, let me turn next to consider how central banks should diagnose the shock, assess its impact on their forecasts and the risks around them and therefore their monetary policy judgements.
 A framework for assessing the impacts of climate shocks
 Here I will draw on the recent NGFS guide on monetary policy strategy that I mentioned earlier footnote [10] . Th
